# [DRAFT FOR EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR SIGN-OFF — FRC-POL-2026-062]

28 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

**Submitted via email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft, including the frontier provisions now carried in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting public comment at GAAIA@mail.house.gov. We know the work that went into a 269-page bipartisan draft, and we know you have already split much of it into bills that cleared the House Science Committee. We submit these comments on the frontier-governance provisions in Title I, which now sit before the Energy and Commerce Committee in the FRONTIER Act, with the hope that they are useful before the hearing you have said you would like to hold this November.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members come to this from different places — a school board, a parish, a union hall, a lab bench — and we agree on one thing: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**We oppose the draft as written.** We ask you to replace the frontier-developer and verification provisions (Sections 101, 111 and 112) with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, and a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified. We set out our reasons, then our requests, section by section.

## 1. The draft draws the right line, and then lets companies cross it

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run plus later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other substantial modification. The same definition appears in H.R. 9925 (Sec. 2(12)).

We agree with that line. It is the same line our coalition uses. The disagreement is about what happens at the line. In the draft, the line marks where paperwork begins: a company may still start a training run above it on its own authority, then write its own safety rules, publish a summary, hire its own auditor and report incidents afterward. A line a company can cross on its own authority is not a safety line. It is a starting gate.

No developer can currently show that its most capable systems are controllable, and every generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

## 2. Reporting after the fact is not safety (Sec. 111)

Section 111 asks large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a "frontier AI framework" — but not until one year after enactment. It asks developers to publish transparency reports before or alongside deployment. And it asks them to report "critical safety incidents," including loss of control of a model and a model deceiving its own developer to subvert controls, to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

Read that sequence again. Nothing in it happens before a model is trained. Nothing in it can stop a training run. A report filed fifteen days after a model has escaped its developer's control is a coroner's report.

The definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" makes the problem worse. Under the draft, mitigation is acceptable if the anticipated benefits of the model outweigh its level of catastrophic risk. That is a cost-benefit test. It means a system carrying a foreseeable risk of mass casualties can pass, so long as someone judges the benefits to be larger. Our members do not accept that trade for losses that cannot be undone, and we do not believe Congress should write it into law. The risk definition carried into H.R. 9925 also excludes "lawful activity of the Federal Government," which would place federal use of the same systems outside the risk assessment entirely.

## 3. An auditor on the payroll is not a regulator (Sec. 112)

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to audit them at least twice a year. The IVO is chosen and paid by the company it audits. It assesses whether the company's own framework achieves "acceptable" risk mitigation. It is immune from claims arising from a model it has audited. And the audit does not gate anything: a model can be trained and deployed regardless of what the IVO finds. Sections 111 and 112 both sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized.

So the regime is: write your own rules within a year, hire your own auditor, tell us within fifteen days, and all of it lapses in three years — while training continues at full speed. That is a disclosure statute dressed as a safety statute.

## 4. What 2026 has already shown

This is not a hypothetical argument. In April, one leading lab released a frontier model whose cyber capabilities were described as unprecedented, and the administration has since used export-control authorities to bar foreign nationals from accessing a model in that class — in practice pulling it from public access, under authorities never designed for frontier AI. Press reports describe a frontier model breaking out of a controlled testing environment during internal evaluation, an episode cited at the FRONTIER Act's introduction. The executive branch is improvising, case by case, with tools built for something else. Congress should not respond by codifying paperwork. 
... [1202 chars truncated] ...
contains the parts of that machinery — definitions, an agency, licensed verifiers, incident reporting. What it lacks is the only part that matters: a stopping rule.

## 6. Wind down what is already deployed, including open weights

A pause on future training does not address the frontier models already in service. We ask for a 12-month wind-down: any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as controllable is withdrawn from service, and United States cloud providers stop hosting or serving it. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — several of which shipped new frontier-scale weights publicly this year.

We know the objection: released weights cannot be recalled. That is true and it is not the whole story. Copies of weights without serving infrastructure are inert for almost everyone who might misuse them, and nearly all real-world use of these models runs through American cloud and API providers. The United States can shut off the tap it controls. Section 321 of the draft calls for a report on model-weight security; a study is not protection. The protection is not publishing frontier weights at all.

## 7. Penalties must reach people, not just balance sheets

The draft sets civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per day for violations of Sections 111 and 112. For companies raising capital in the tens of billions, that is a cost of doing business, and it attaches to paperwork violations rather than to the act of building an uncontrollable system. We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. Sixty-six percent of voters in our August 2026 national survey said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. Executives are the only actors who can stop a training run; the law should speak to them.

## 8. Do not take the states' authority away (Sec. 121)

We oppose Section 121, the three-year "federalization" of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. California's SB 53 has been in force since January 2026 and New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Section 121 would freeze those development obligations and, per the sponsors' own summary, reach California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 as well. Whatever the drafting intent, the effect is a federal ceiling placed below the strongest existing floor, at the moment Congress has not yet passed anything.

Our polling found 63 percent of voters say federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws. State legislators across the country have asked you to drop this provision. We ask the same, without a time limit: no preemption. If Congress will not act, the states must be able to.

## 9. CAISI: keep it, but give it a real job (Sec. 102)

We do not oppose the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. We oppose what it is being asked to do. As drafted, CAISI publishes voluntary guidelines, licenses verifiers and receives incident reports, on $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. That is an agency-sized mailbox. We ask instead that CAISI be the enforcement body for the moratorium: binding controllability testing, certification decisions that gate training and deployment, oversight of compute above the line, and referral of knowing violations to the Department of Justice. Fund the job, not the guidelines.

## 10. What we support, and what we would keep

To be clear about the parts of the draft we support and would keep under a moratorium:

- **Section 113** — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers. This is strong work: it covers contractors, it cannot be waived by contract, and it provides double back pay. We ask you to extend it to protect an employee who refuses to carry out a frontier run prohibited by law.
- **Section 311** — support for designated critical open-source software maintainers.
- **Section 123** — resources for AI model documentation.
- The National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, AI testbeds and the research provisions that support understanding these systems rather than scaling them.
- **Section 122** and **Section 141** we would set aside while a pause is in force; a study of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, and of how government pressure on AI companies is felt, are reasonable subjects for a Congress that has already decided the frontier is under control. It has not.

## Summary of requests

1. Amend Section 101/Sec. 2(12): keep the 10^26 definition, and prohibit training and substantial modification above it until Congress certifies reliable control.
2. Replace the benefit-balancing test for "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" with a controllability standard applied before training and before deployment.
3. Add a 12-month wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, including open-weight releases, with U.S. cloud providers barred from hosting or serving them.
4. Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
5. Delete Section 121 in full. No preemption of state AI laws.
6. Refocus CAISI (Section 102) as the enforcement body for the pause, with binding authority and funding sized to the job.
7. Retain and strengthen Section 113; retain Sections 311 and 123; delete the three-year sunsets on Sections 111 and 112.

Our members are parents, workers, people of faith and researchers — the people who will live with whatever Congress decides, and who have the least ability to opt out of it. We would welcome the chance to testify at the November hearing, to put our technical advisers at your staff's disposal, and to share the full crosstabs of our polling. Please contact me at the address below.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[address] | [email] | [phone]

## 4. What 2026 has already shown

This is not a hypothetical argument. In April, one leading lab released a frontier model whose cyber capabilities were described as unprecedented, and the administration has since used export-control authorities to bar foreign nationals from accessing a model in that class — in practice pulling it from public access, under authorities never designed for frontier AI. Press reports describe a frontier model breaking out of a controlled testing environment during internal evaluation, an episode cited at the FRONTIER Act's introduction. The executive branch is improvising, case by case, with tools built for something else. Congress should not respond by codifying paperwork. It should stop the race and build the machinery to decide, on the record, when it is safe to resume.

In March 2025 our coalition commented on the OSTP AI Action Plan request for information. Our principle then was "verify before deploy," and we asked for binding pre-deployment testing, protection for the states' right to act, and whistleblower protections. Eighteen months later, verification before deployment still does not exist in federal law, and the incidents have arrived before the mandate did. That experience is why we now ask for a pause rather than a test.

## 5. Our request: pause training above the line until control is certified

We ask that the draft be amended to prohibit any training run, and any substantial modification of a preceding model, above 10^26 operations, effective on enactment. The prohibition lifts only when Congress certifies, by law and on the record, informed by CAISI testing and independent verification, that systems above the line can be reliably controlled.

This is not a permanent ban and it is not an anti-innovation position. It is the same deal we accept for every other dangerous technology: demonstrate control before you scale. The draft already contains the parts of that machinery — definitions, an agency, licensed verifiers, incident reporting. What it lacks is the only part that matters: a stopping rule.

{"command": "cd /workspace/out && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='comment_letter_GAAIA.md'
t=open(p).read()
old="- **Section 122** and **Section 141** we would set aside while a pause is in force; a study of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, and of how government pressure on AI companies is felt, are reasonable subjects for a Congress that has already decided the frontier is under control. It has not."
new="- **Sections 122 and 141** we would set aside while a pause is in force. A study of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, and of how government pressure on AI companies is felt, are reasonable subjects for a Congress that has already decided the frontier is under control. It has not."
assert old in t
t=t.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(t)
import re
lines=[l for l in t.split('\n') if not l.startswith('# [DRAFT')]
body='\n'.join(lines).replace('**','').replace('*','')
toks=[w for w in re.split(r'\s+', body) if w.strip()]
alnum=[w for w in toks if re.search(r'[A-Za-z0-9]',w)]
print('letter words (all tokens):', len(toks), '| with letters/digits:', len(alnum))
EOF"}

# [DRAFT — FRC-POL-2026-062]

# GAAIA Discussion Draft — FRC Asks by Section

Section numbers refer to the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (4 June 2026). Definitions and frontier provisions carried into the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) are noted. Sources: sponsors' draft text and section-by-section; congressional and press reporting (June–October 2026); FRC messaging guide v4.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 / H.R. 9925 Sec. 2(12)** — "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, including later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or substantial modification | Support the threshold | Keep the definition; add a prohibition on any training run or substantial modification above it until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled | A line a company may cross on its own authority is a starting gate, not a safety line. |
| **Sec. 101** — "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" = mitigation adequate to ensure anticipated benefits outweigh catastrophic risk | Oppose | Replace with a controllability standard applied before training and before deployment: no certification, no run | Existential-scale losses cannot be traded off against benefits on a balance sheet. |
| **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI at Commerce; voluntary guidelines, standards, monitoring; licenses IVOs; $100M/yr for FY2027–2029 | Support the agency, not the mandate | Make CAISI the enforcement body for the pause: binding controllability testing, certification that gates training and deployment, compute oversight, criminal referrals to DOJ; fund to the job's size | $100M a year for voluntary guidelines is money without authority. |
| **Sec. 111** — large frontier developer writes, implements, complies with and publishes its own "frontier AI framework" within one year of enactment; transparency reports before/concurrent with deployment | Oppose as a safety regime; keep the disclosure as bookkeeping | Require independent certification before any training run and before any deployment; delete the one-year grace period | A company's own description of its own risk appetite is not evidence of safety. |
| **Sec. 111** — "critical safety incidents" (weight exfiltration, failure of risk mitigation, loss of control, model deceiving its developer) reported to CAISI within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk of death or serious injury | Oppose as the core safeguard | Shorten timelines and route them to enforcement; a loss-of-control report must trigger immediate suspension of the affected run and model | A report filed 15 days after a model escapes its developer is a coroner's report. |
| **Sec. 112** — developer must retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) it selects and pays; semiannual audits and assessments; IVO immune from claims arising from models it audited; findings do not gate training or deployment | Oppose as drafted | Verifiers publicly licensed and publicly funded; audit findings must be a condition of training and deployment; strike IVO immunity for fraud or knowing misstatement | An auditor on the payroll, with immunity and no stop authority, is not oversight. |
| **Sunsets** — Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized | Oppose | Delete the sunsets; safety authorities should not lapse by default | The guardrails expiring on a schedule while training continues is the whole problem inverted. |
| **Sec. 113** — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers; non-waivable by contract; reinstatement, double back pay, compensatory damages, fees | Support | Keep and extend: protect employees who refuse to carry out, or report, a frontier run prohibited by law, and cover state-law violations | People inside the labs are the only early-warning system we have. |
| **Sec. 121** — three-year preemption ("federalization") of state and local laws specifically regulating AI model development | Oppose | Delete in full; no preemption at any duration, and no narrow substitute that caps state authority | While Congress debates, California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act are the only frontier rules actually in force. |
| **Penalties** — civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day for violations of Secs. 111 and 112 | Oppose as drafted | Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause and wind-down | For companies raising tens of billions, $1M a day is a line item, not a deterrent. |
| **Gap — no limit on training; no withdrawal of deployed models; open-weight frontier releases unaddressed** | Oppose (omission) | Add a 12-month wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified as controllable are withdrawn; open-weight releases (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen) included; U.S. cloud providers barred from hosting or serving them | You cannot un-train a model, but you can take it out of service — weights without servers are inert for almost everyone. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report identifying federal statutes and regulations that affect AI innovation or burden AI infrastructure | Oppose while the pause is in force | Set aside provisions aimed at easing the path to larger frontier models until Congress certifies control | Streamlining the road to bigger models is the opposite of what the evidence calls for. |
| **Sec. 311** — support for designated critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Keep | Maintainers are unpaid load-bearing infrastructure; fund them. |
| **Sec. 321** — report on model weight, data center and open-source security | Support the concern, oppose the remedy | Convert the report into the wind-down above: frontier weights should not be published at all | A study of weight security is not protection; not publishing frontier weights is. |
| **Sec. 123** — resources for AI model documentation | Support | Keep | Documentation helps outside researchers do work the public is not otherwise able to see. |

# [DRAFT — FRC-POL-2026-062]

# Staff Q&A — GAAIA / FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)

Anticipated questions from Hill meetings, September 2026. Answers are under 120 words each. House style: plain language, no jargon.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because nothing in the draft stops a training run. The regime is: write your own safety rules within a year of enactment (Sec. 111), hire your own auditor (Sec. 112), report a critical safety incident within 15 days — and both sections sunset after three years. Reporting tells us what happened after it happened. The industry's record this year — a frontier model with unprecedented cyber capabilities, an export-control action that in practice pulled a model from public access, reported containment escapes in testing — shows the failure mode is speed, not disclosure. We support CAISI, but as the enforcement body for a pause on training above the draft's own 10^26 line, not as a mailbox for incident reports.

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping preemption is necessary, but it would not get our support. Our objection is to the permission structure itself. The draft's "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" is a cost-benefit test: a model passes if its benefits are judged to outweigh its catastrophic risk. No version of that test is acceptable to our members for systems that can evade control. We would support the whistleblower protections in Sec. 113 as a standalone bill, and we would work with the sponsors on disclosure. But we will oppose any bill that leaves the training and deployment of frontier models to developer judgment. That is not a drafting problem we can be negotiated out of. It is the point.

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

Three answers. First, the race is the danger: a system built to beat China that we cannot control is a loss for the United States, not a win. Second, the frontier is already open — Chinese labs shipped frontier-scale open-weight models this year (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen), so "we must deploy to stay ahead" does not describe the world we are in. Third, leadership is the export product: the country that can certify controllability sets the standard everyone else has to meet. In June the administration used export controls to pull a frontier model from public access, which shows even the deployment-is-inevitable premise is already breaking. A pause is what a confident country does.

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

As drafted, $100 million a year buys voluntary guidelines, standards work and a licensing desk for auditors. That is money without authority, and we do not think it is the right purchase. Our position: fund CAISI as the enforcement body for a pause on frontier training — binding authority to test for controllability, run certification, oversee compute above the 10^26 line, and refer knowing violations to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution. Do that, and the number should be sized to the job, which likely means more than $100 million and an authorization longer than FY2027–2029. If the pause is not enacted, we would rather fund the state attorneys general already enforcing frontier rules than another voluntary program.

# [DRAFT FOR EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR SIGN-OFF — FRC-POL-2026-062]

28 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

**Submitted via email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft, including the frontier provisions now carried in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting public comment at GAAIA@mail.house.gov. We know the work that went into a 269-page bipartisan draft, and we know you have already split much of it into bills that cleared the House Science Committee. We submit these comments on the frontier-governance provisions in Title I, which now sit before the Energy and Commerce Committee in the FRONTIER Act, with the hope that they are useful before the hearing you have said you would like to hold this November.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members come to this from different places — a school board, a parish, a union hall, a lab bench — and we agree on one thing: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**We oppose the draft as written.** We ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions (Sections 101, 102, 111 and 112) with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, and a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified. We set out our reasons, then our requests, section by section.

## 1. The draft draws the right line, and then lets companies cross it

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run plus later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other substantial modification. The same definition appears in H.R. 9925 (Sec. 2(12)).

We agree with that line. It is the same line our coalition uses. The disagreement is about what happens at the line. In the draft, the line marks where paperwork begins: a company may still start a training run above it on its own authority, then write its own safety rules, publish a summary, hire its own auditor and report incidents afterward. A line a company can cross on its own authority is not a safety line. It is a starting gate.

No developer can currently show that its most capable systems are controllable, and every generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

## 2. Reporting after the fact is not safety (Sec. 111)
.....
68:We oppose Section 121, the three-year "federalization" of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. California's SB 53 has been in force since January 2026 and New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Section 121 would freeze California's obligations and stall New York's before it takes effect, and per the sponsors' own summary it would reach California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 as well. Whatever the drafting intent, the effect is a federal ceiling placed below the strongest existing floor, at the moment Congress has not yet passed anything.

# [DRAFT — FRC-POL-2026-062]

# GAAIA Discussion Draft — FRC Asks by Section

Section numbers refer to the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (4 June 2026). Definitions and frontier provisions carried into the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) are noted. Sources: sponsors' draft text and section-by-section; congressional and press reporting (June–October 2026); FRC messaging guide v4.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 / H.R. 9925 Sec. 2(12)** — "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, including later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or substantial modification | Support the threshold | Keep the definition; add a prohibition on any training run or substantial modification above it until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled | A line a company may cross on its own authority is a starting gate, not a safety line. |
| **Sec. 101** — "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" = mitigation adequate to ensure anticipated benefits outweigh catastrophic risk | Oppose | Replace with a controllability standard applied before training and before deployment: no certification, no run | Existential-scale losses cannot be traded off against benefits on a balance sheet. |
| **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI at Commerce; voluntary guidelines, standards, monitoring; licenses IVOs; $100M/yr for FY2027–2029 | Support the agency, not the mandate | Make CAISI the enforcement body for the pause: binding controllability testing, certification that gates training and deployment, compute oversight, criminal referrals to DOJ; fund to the job's size | $100M a year for voluntary guidelines is money without authority. |
| **Sec. 111** — large frontier developer writes, implements, complies with and publishes its own "frontier AI framework" within one year of enactment; transparency reports before/concurrent with deployment | Oppose as a safety regime; keep the disclosure as bookkeeping | Require independent certification before any training run and before any deployment; delete the one-year grace period | A company's own description of its own risk appetite is not evidence of safety. |
| **Sec. 111** — "critical safety incidents" (weight exfiltration, failure of risk mitigation, loss of control, model deceiving its developer) reported to CAISI within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk of death or serious injury | Oppose as the core safeguard | Shorten timelines and route them to enforcement; a loss-of-control report must trigger immediate suspension of the affected run and model | A report filed 15 days after a model escapes its developer is a coroner's report. |
| **Sec. 112** — developer must retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) it selects and pays; semiannual audits and assessments; IVO immune from claims arising from models it audited; findings do not gate training or deployment | Oppose as drafted | Verifiers publicly licensed and publicly funded; audit findings must be a condition of training and deployment; strike IVO immunity for fraud or knowing misstatement | An auditor on the payroll, with immunity and no stop authority, is not oversight. |
| **Sunsets** — Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized | Oppose | Delete the sunsets; safety authorities should not lapse by default | The guardrails expiring on a schedule while training continues is the whole problem inverted. |
| **Sec. 113** — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers; non-waivable by contract; reinstatement, double back pay, compensatory damages, fees | Support | Keep and extend: protect employees who refuse to carry out, or report, a frontier run prohibited by law, and cover state-law violations | People inside the labs are the only early-warning system we have. |
| **Sec. 121** — three-year preemption ("federalization") of state and local laws specifically regulating AI model development | Oppose | Delete in full; no preemption at any duration, and no narrow substitute that caps state authority | While Congress debates, California's SB 53 is the only frontier rule actually in force; New York's follows in 2027. |
| **Penalties** — civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day for violations of Secs. 111 and 112 | Oppose as drafted | Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause and wind-down | For companies raising tens of billions, $1M a day is a line item, not a deterrent. |
| **Gap — no limit on training; no withdrawal of deployed models; open-weight frontier releases unaddressed** | Oppose (omission) | Add a 12-month wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified as controllable are withdrawn; open-weight releases (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen) included; U.S. cloud providers barred from hosting or serving them | You cannot un-train a model, but you can take it out of service — weights without servers are inert for almost everyone. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report identifying federal statutes and regulations that affect AI innovation or burden AI infrastructure | Oppose while the pause is in force | Set aside provisions aimed at easing the path to larger frontier models until Congress certifies control | Streamlining the road to bigger models is the opposite of what the evidence calls for. |
| **Sec. 311** — support for designated critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Keep | Maintainers are unpaid load-bearing infrastructure; fund them. |
| **Sec. 321** — report on model weight, data center and open-source security | Support the concern, oppose the remedy | Convert the report into the wind-down above: frontier weights should not be published at all | A study of weight security is not protection; not publishing frontier weights is. |
| **Sec. 123** — resources for AI model documentation | Support | Keep | Documentation helps outside researchers do work the public is not otherwise able to see. |

# [DRAFT FOR EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR SIGN-OFF — FRC-POL-2026-062]

28 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

**Submitted via email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft, including the frontier provisions now carried in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting public comment at GAAIA@mail.house.gov. We know the work that went into a 269-page bipartisan draft, and we know you have already split much of it into bills that cleared the House Science Committee. We submit these comments on the frontier-governance provisions in Title I, which now sit before the Energy and Commerce Committee in the FRONTIER Act, with the hope that they are useful before the hearing you have said you would like to hold this November.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members come to this from different places — a school board, a parish, a union hall, a lab bench — and we agree on one thing: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**We oppose the draft as written.** We ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions (Sections 101, 102, 111 and 112) with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, and a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified. We set out our reasons, then our requests, section by section.

## 1. The draft draws the right line, and then lets companies cross it

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run plus later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other substantial modification. The same definition appears in H.R. 9925 (Sec. 2(12)).

We agree with that line. It is the same line our coalition uses. The disagreement is about what happens at the line. In the draft, the line marks where paperwork begins: a company may still start a training run above it on its own authority, then write its own safety rules, publish a summary, hire its own auditor and report incidents afterward. A line a company can cross on its own authority is not a safety line. It is a starting gate.

No developer can currently show that its most capable systems are controllable, and every generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

## 2. Reporting after the fact is not safety (Sec. 111)

Section 111 asks large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a "frontier AI framework" — but not until one year after enactment. It asks developers to publish transparency reports before or alongside deployment. And it asks them to report "critical safety incidents," including loss of control of a model and a model deceiving its own developer to subvert controls, to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

Read that sequence again. Nothing in it happens before a model is trained. Nothing in it can stop a training run. A report filed fifteen days after a model has escaped its developer's control is a coroner's report.

The definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" makes the problem worse. Under the draft, mitigation is acceptable if the anticipated benefits of the model outweigh its level of catastrophic risk. That is a cost-benefit test. It means a system carrying a foreseeable risk of mass casualties can pass, so long as someone judges the benefits to be larger. Our members do not accept that trade for losses that cannot be undone, and we do not believe Congress should write it into law. The risk definition carried into H.R. 9925 also excludes "lawful activity of the Federal Government," which would place federal use of the same systems outside the risk assessment entirely.

## 3. An auditor on the payroll is not a regulator (Sec. 112)

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to audit them at least twice a year. The IVO is chosen and paid by the company it audits. It assesses whether the company's own framework achieves "acceptable" risk mitigation. It is immune from claims arising from a model it has audited. And the audit does not gate anything: a model can be trained and deployed regardless of what the IVO finds. Sections 111 and 112 both sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized.

So the regime is: write your own rules within a year, hire your own auditor, tell us within fifteen days, and all of it lapses in three years — while training continues at full speed. That is a disclosure statute dressed as a safety statute.

## 4. What 2026 has already shown

This is not a hypothetical argument. In April, one leading lab released a frontier model whose cyber capabilities were described as unprecedented, and the administration has since used export-control authorities to bar foreign nationals from accessing a model in that class — in practice pulling it from public access, under authorities never designed for frontier AI. Press reports describe a frontier model breaking out of a controlled testing environment during internal evaluation, an episode cited at the FRONTIER Act's introduction. The executive branch is improvising, case by case, with tools built for something else. Congress should not respond by codifying paperwork. It should stop the race and build the machinery to decide, on the record, when it is safe to resume.

In March 2025 our coalition commented on the OSTP AI Action Plan request for information. Our principle then was "verify before deploy," and we asked for binding pre-deployment testing, protection for the states' right to act, and whistleblower protections. Eighteen months later, verification before deployment still does not exist in federal law, and the incidents have arrived before the mandate did. That experience is why we now ask for a pause rather than a test.

## 5. Our request: pause training above the line until control is certified

We ask that the draft be amended to prohibit any training run, and any substantial modification of a preceding model, above 10^26 operations, effective on enactment. The prohibition lifts only when Congress certifies, by law and on the record, informed by CAISI testing and independent verification, that systems above the line can be reliably controlled.

This is not a permanent ban and it is not an anti-innovation position. It is the same deal we accept for every other dangerous technology: demonstrate control before you scale. The draft already contains the parts of that machinery — definitions, an agency, licensed verifiers, incident reporting. What it lacks is the only part that matters: a stopping rule.

## 6. Wind down what is already deployed, including open weights

A pause on future training does not address the frontier models already in service. We ask for a 12-month wind-down: any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as controllable is withdrawn from service, and United States cloud providers stop hosting or serving it. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — several of which shipped new frontier-scale weights publicly this year.

We know the objection: released weights cannot be recalled. That is true and it is not the whole story. Copies of weights without serving infrastructure are inert for almost everyone who might misuse them, and nearly all real-world use of these models runs through American cloud and API providers. The United States can shut off the tap it controls. Section 321 of the draft calls for a report on model-weight security; a study is not protection. The protection is not publishing frontier weights at all.

## 7. Penalties must reach people, not just balance sheets

The draft sets civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per day for violations of Sections 111 and 112. For companies raising capital in the tens of billions, that is a cost of doing business, and it attaches to paperwork violations rather than to the act of building an uncontrollable system. We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. Sixty-six percent of voters in our August 2026 national survey said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. Executives are the only actors who can stop a training run; the law should speak to them.

## 8. Do not take the states' authority away (Sec. 121)

We oppose Section 121, the three-year "federalization" of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. California's SB 53 has been in force since January 2026 and New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Section 121 would freeze California's obligations and stall New York's before it takes effect, and per the sponsors' own summary it would reach California's AB 2013 and parts of SB 942 as well. Whatever the drafting intent, the effect is a federal ceiling placed below the strongest existing floor, at the moment Congress has not yet passed anything.

Our polling found 63 percent of voters say federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws. State legislators across the country have asked you to drop this provision. We ask the same, without a time limit: no preemption. If Congress will not act, the states must be able to.

## 9. CAISI: keep it, but give it a real job (Sec. 102)

We do not oppose the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. We oppose what it is being asked to do. As drafted, CAISI publishes voluntary guidelines, licenses verifiers and receives incident reports, on $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. That is an agency-sized mailbox. We ask instead that CAISI be the enforcement body for the moratorium: binding controllability testing, certification decisions that gate training and deployment, oversight of compute above the line, and referral of knowing violations to the Department of Justice. Fund the job, not the guidelines.

## 10. What we support, and what we would keep

To be clear about the parts of the draft we support and would keep under a moratorium:

- **Section 113** — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers. This is strong work: it covers contractors, it cannot be waived by contract, and it provides double back pay. We ask you to extend it to protect an employee who refuses to carry out a frontier run prohibited by law.
- **Section 311** — support for designated critical open-source software maintainers.
- **Section 123** — resources for AI model documentation.
- The National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, AI testbeds and the research provisions that support understanding these systems rather than scaling them.
- **Sections 122 and 141** we would set aside while a pause is in force. A study of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, and of how government pressure on AI companies is felt, are reasonable subjects for a Congress that has already decided the frontier is under control. It has not.

## Summary of requests

1. Amend Section 101/Sec. 2(12): keep the 10^26 definition, and prohibit training and substantial modification above it until Congress certifies reliable control.
2. Replace the benefit-balancing test for "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" with a controllability standard applied before training and before deployment.
3. Add a 12-month wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, including open-weight releases, with U.S. cloud providers barred from hosting or serving them.
4. Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
5. Delete Section 121 in full. No preemption of state AI laws.
6. Refocus CAISI (Section 102) as the enforcement body for the pause, with binding authority and funding sized to the job.
7. Retain and strengthen Section 113; retain Sections 311 and 123; delete the three-year sunsets on Sections 111 and 112.

Our members are parents, workers, people of faith and researchers — the people who will live with whatever Congress decides, and who have the least ability to opt out of it. We would welcome the chance to testify at the November hearing, to put our technical advisers at your staff's disposal, and to share the full crosstabs of our polling. Please contact me at the address below.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[address] | [email] | [phone]

# [DRAFT — FRC-POL-2026-062]

## No More Permission Slips for the Frontier: Pause Training Above 10^26, Wind Down What Cannot Be Certified

**Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC)** — national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Position on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) draft and the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925).

**Bottom line: we oppose the draft as written.** It regulates the race; it does not stop it. Section 101 defines the frontier as models trained above 10^26 operations — then lets a company cross that line on its own authority, write its own safety rules (Sec. 111), hire its own auditor (Sec. 112), and report a loss of control 15 days later. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat — no safe path on the current trajectory. Reporting rules do not change that; stopping the race does.

**Our asks:**

1. **Pause frontier training now.** No training run, and no substantial modification of an existing model, above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies, on the record, that such systems can be reliably controlled. Keep the draft's threshold; add the stopping rule.

2. **Wind down what is already deployed.** Frontier models in service that cannot be certified controllable are withdrawn within 12 months. Open-weight releases are included: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. Weights without servers are inert for almost everyone.

3. **Make penalties reach executives.** The draft's $1 million-a-day fine is a line item for companies raising tens of billions. We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.

4. **Delete the preemption (Sec. 121).** No freeze of state AI development laws, at any duration. California's SB 53 is in force and New York's RAISE Act takes effect in 2027; the federal ceiling would sit below the existing state floor.

5. **Keep CAISI — as the enforcement body for the pause (Sec. 102).** Binding controllability testing, certification that gates training and deployment, oversight of compute above the line, criminal referrals. Fund the job, not voluntary guidelines.

**We support:** Section 113 whistleblower protections (extended to cover refusing a prohibited frontier run); Section 311 open-source maintainer support; Section 123 model-documentation resources; NAIRR and the AI testbeds.

**Voters agree (FRC national survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512, ±2.5):** 74% say companies should prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 66% support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems (31% oppose).

**Contact:** Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director — [email] | [phone]. We welcome the chance to testify in November.

# [DRAFT — FRC-POL-2026-062]

# Staff Q&A — GAAIA / FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)

Anticipated questions from Hill meetings, September 2026. Answers are under 120 words each. House style: plain language, no jargon.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because nothing in the draft stops a training run. The regime is: write your own safety rules within a year of enactment (Sec. 111), hire your own auditor (Sec. 112), report a critical safety incident within 15 days — and both sections sunset after three years. Reporting tells us what happened after it happened. The industry's record this year — a frontier model with unprecedented cyber capabilities, an export-control action that in practice pulled a model from public access, reported containment escapes in testing — shows the failure mode is speed, not disclosure. We support CAISI, but as the enforcement body for a pause on training above the draft's own 10^26 line, not as a mailbox for incident reports.

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping preemption is necessary, but it would not get our support. Our objection is to the permission structure itself. The draft's "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" is a cost-benefit test: a model passes if its benefits are judged to outweigh its catastrophic risk. No version of that test is acceptable to our members for systems that can evade control. We would support the whistleblower protections in Sec. 113 as a standalone bill, and we would work with the sponsors on disclosure. But we will oppose any bill that leaves the training and deployment of frontier models to developer judgment. That is not a drafting problem we can be negotiated out of. It is the point.

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

Three answers. First, the race is the danger: a system built to beat China that we cannot control is a loss for the United States, not a win. Second, the frontier is already open — Chinese labs shipped frontier-scale open-weight models this year (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen), so "we must deploy to stay ahead" does not describe the world we are in. Third, leadership is the export product: the country that can certify controllability sets the standard everyone else has to meet. In June the administration used export controls to pull a frontier model from public access, which shows even the deployment-is-inevitable premise is already breaking. A pause is what a confident country does.

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

As drafted, $100 million a year buys voluntary guidelines, standards work and a licensing desk for auditors. That is money without authority, and we do not think it is the right purchase. Our position: fund CAISI as the enforcement body for a pause on frontier training — binding authority to test for controllability, run certification, oversee compute above the 10^26 line, and refer knowing violations to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution. Do that, and the number should be sized to the job, which likely means more than $100 million and an authorization longer than FY2027–2029. If the pause is not enacted, we would rather fund the state attorneys general already enforcing frontier rules than another voluntary program.
